paras: The Charleston, Illinois, vigilance committee whippings and expulsions took place in March 1881, when masked vigilantes at Charleston, in Coles County, hung and whipped three men accused of belonging to a gang of thieves and house-burners and then ordered some twenty other people out of town. No one was reported killed, and nearly all of those warned left within a day. The story ran in papers across the country, and several editors cited it as evidence that lynching was not confined to the South.

According to dispatches from Charleston, the vigilantes meant to rid the area of a gang of "desperadoes and their women" who had burned houses and haystacks, stolen or hamstrung cattle and horses, robbed, and "even murdered" for two years. These charges came from the vigilantes' side, and the coverage reports no prosecution of anyone for them. The three men seized were described as returned convicts from the Joliet penitentiary and as the gang's leaders.

On Thursday night, March 17, a band of masked men, reported as a vigilance committee of seventy-five, took Myron Martin, Wm. Sweeny, alias "English Bill," and Charles Scott, alias "Grasshopper," from their beds. One account says the three were hung in a tree and whipped until "life was nearly extinct," then let down and ordered to leave the country. The vigilantes warned that they would be killed if they returned.

The next night printed bills were posted around Charleston warning some twenty people, about half of them women, to leave or be "regulated" by the vigilantes. The Chicago Tribune listed Joe Vanderin Jr., Cass Farrell, Mary Hyatt and "English Bill" among them, while another dispatch named Rose Davis, Joe Leele, Eliza Ritter, Rob Scott, Meach Thompson, Mary Hoat and Laura Duncan. By the following day most of those named had fled, and the Lancaster Intelligencer reported that every one of them had left.

A Chicago Tribune dispatch reported great excitement in Charleston over the vigilantes' work and said they were "determined on thorough work." No report of arrests, an inquest, or any official action against the vigilantes appears in the coverage.

The first word came in a St. Louis Republican special from Charleston, which ran on March 19 in the Memphis Daily Appeal under the headline "A Gentle Hint to Leave" and in the St. Paul Daily Globe. The follow-up dispatch about the posted bills appeared on March 20 and 21 in the New-York Tribune, the Chicago Tribune, the Memphis Daily Appeal ("Getting Rid of a Bad Crowd") and the Wheeling Register. Shorter items naming the three men ran into April in papers from Ohio and New Hampshire to Arkansas.

Most papers repeated the vigilantes' description of their targets without comment, and some took it further: the Stark County Democrat's headline was "Leaving the Country for the Country's Good," and the Morris Tribune called the men "bad citizens." No paper gave a race for anyone involved.

Editors in Pennsylvania and Tennessee turned the case into a sectional argument. The Lancaster Intelligencer headed its item "Regulating Things in Logan's State" and, as quoted by the Clearfield Republican, said the events had "stained the soil and shamed the law" of Senator John A. Logan's Illinois, though the men were probably "great rascals"; had such things happened in the South, it argued, Republicans would have blamed politics. The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle in Tennessee wrote that lynching was "not entirely confined to the South" and asked to hear from the Chicago papers on "these Southern outrages."

Most accounts place the whipping on Thursday night, March 17, but the Perrysburg Journal dated it "the 18th," the date of the first dispatch. The dated dispatches say the bills went up the night after the whipping, while the Lancaster account says Saturday, and the number warned is given as twenty, fifteen, or four names "and about ten others." The Clarksville editorial said the men were whipped and then hung, but it reports no deaths, and the fuller accounts say the three survived and were driven out.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'A Gentle Hint to Leave' and 'Getting Rid of a Bad Crowd' carried the targets' characterization as thieves, house-burners and 'desperadoes' without comment.
The Stark County Democrat headed its dispatch 'Leaving the Country for the Country's Good', and the Morris Tribune called the targets 'bad citizens'.

The Lancaster Intelligencer, quoted by the Clearfield Republican, said the events 'stained the soil and shamed the law' of Logan's Illinois while granting the men were probably 'great rascals', and used the case to accuse Republicans of exploiting Southern violence.
The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle cited the case to show lynching was 'not entirely confined to the South' and challenged the Chicago papers.
